name: Charles K. Kao
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Kao earned his BSc in electrical engineering in 1957 (age 24) and worked as a graduate/trainee engineer at Standard Telephones & Cables. His seminal fiber optics work was published in 1966 (age 33) and his PhD was awarded in 1965 (age 32).
early_history_summary: Born in Shanghai in 1933 to a lawyer father who was a professor at Soochow University, Kao moved to Hong Kong in 1948 and studied at St. Joseph's College before going to England in 1953. He earned a BSc in electrical engineering from Woolwich Polytechnic (University of London) in 1957 and joined Standard Telephones & Cables as a trainee engineer, rotating through divisions before settling in the microwave division. He transferred to Standard Telecommunication Laboratories in 1960.
family_context_summary: Father was a lawyer with a JD from the University of Michigan who became a professor at Soochow University; family moved from Shanghai to Hong Kong in 1948, suggesting a middle-class professional background that supported overseas study.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a law professor, not directly in engineering or technology; no evidence of parental domain expertise in Kao's field.
evidence_summary: Kao's path to his Nobel-winning fiber optics work began with a conventional engineering education at Woolwich Polytechnic (BSc 1957) followed by industrial experience at STC. By age 26 he was a junior engineer with no notable publications or discoveries. His groundbreaking 1966 paper with Hockham on glass fiber communications came at age 33, well beyond the age-26 threshold.

name: François Englert
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Englert earned an electromechanical engineering degree in 1955 (age 23) and a physics master's in 1958 (age 26). His PhD was awarded in 1959 (age 27) and his seminal Higgs mechanism paper with Robert Brout was published in 1964 (age 32).
early_history_summary: Born in 1932 in Etterbeek, Belgium to a Jewish family that emigrated from Poland, Englert survived the Holocaust by hiding in orphanages and with local families during the German occupation. After the war he excelled at mathematics and studied electromechanical engineering at the Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), graduating in 1955, then switched to physics, earning a master's in 1958. He worked as an assistant at ULB to finance his physics studies.
family_context_summary: Born to a Jewish family of Polish immigrants in Belgium; family survived the Holocaust in hiding. No evidence of financial privilege; childhood was marked by wartime persecution and displacement.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents were Polish Jewish immigrants with no noted academic or scientific background.
evidence_summary: Englert's early life was shaped by the Holocaust, which disrupted his childhood education. He pursued engineering then physics at ULB, earning a master's by 1958. His PhD came in 1959 at age 27, followed by a postdoc at Cornell with Robert Brout. His Nobel-winning work on spontaneous symmetry breaking was published in 1964 at age 32, far beyond the age-26 threshold.

name: Jules A. Hoffmann
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Hoffmann published a minor paper on waterbugs at age 17 but was a research assistant at CNRS by age 26 (1967), having not yet completed his PhD (awarded 1969, age 28). His seminal work on insect innate immunity came in the 1970s-80s.
early_history_summary: Born in 1941 in Echternach, Luxembourg, Hoffmann accompanied his father, a high school teacher and amateur entomologist, on insect-collecting trips from an early age, publishing his first paper on waterbugs at 17. He studied biology and chemistry at the University of Strasbourg (1961-1965) and became a CNRS research assistant in 1964, working toward his PhD under Pierre Joly on insect endocrine control.
family_context_summary: Father was a high school teacher who spent spare time collecting and describing insects, providing early domain exposure but not financial privilege.
evidence_summary: Hoffmann benefited from his father's entomology hobby, publishing a minor paper at 17, but his PhD was not completed until 1969 (age 28). His Nobel-winning research on Drosophila innate immunity began in the 1970s and produced key results in the 1980s-90s, well beyond age 26. The early waterbug paper, while notable for his age, was not a seminal publication.

name: Niklaus Wirth
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Wirth earned a BSc from ETH Zurich in 1959 (age 25) and an MSc from Université Laval in 1960 (age 26). His PhD from UC Berkeley came in 1963 (age 29) and his influential languages (Euler, Pascal) were developed in the 1960s-70s.
early_history_summary: Born in 1934 in Winterthur, Switzerland, Wirth developed an early interest in technology, building radios and amplifiers as a child. He studied electrical engineering at ETH Zurich (1954-1958), then earned an MSc at Université Laval in Canada in 1960 before pursuing a PhD at UC Berkeley under Harry Huskey, completing it in 1963. He became an assistant professor at Stanford in 1963.
family_context_summary: Son of Hedwig (née Keller) and Walter Wirth, a high school teacher. No evidence of significant financial privilege or disadvantage.
evidence_summary: Wirth's early path was a conventional academic trajectory through ETH Zurich, Laval, and UC Berkeley. By age 26 he held only an MSc. His PhD (1963) led to the Euler language, but his most influential work, Pascal, came in 1970 at age 36. No seminal publication or notable product by age 26.

name: Georg Bednorz
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Bednorz completed his master's degree in mineralogy/crystallography from the University of Münster in 1976 (age 26). His PhD from ETH Zurich came in 1982 (age 32) and his Nobel-winning discovery of high-temperature superconductivity was in 1986 (age 36).
early_history_summary: Born in 1950 in Neuenkirchen, Germany, Bednorz developed an early interest in mechanics and chemistry. He started studying chemistry at the University of Münster in 1968 but switched to crystallography/mineralogy. He spent summers at the IBM Zurich Research Lab (1972-1974), where he met K. Alex Müller, setting the course for his future career. He completed his diploma in 1976 and began his PhD at ETH Zurich in 1977.
family_context_summary: Parents were Anton Bednorz, an elementary school teacher, and Elisabeth, a piano teacher, both refugees from Silesia during WWII. Modest professional family background.
evidence_summary: Bednorz's early career was a standard academic path through Münster and ETH Zurich, with valuable summer internships at IBM Zurich. By age 26 he had only a master's degree. His Nobel-winning discovery of high-Tc superconductivity came in 1986 at age 36, a full decade after the age-26 threshold.

name: Pierre-Gilles de Gennes
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; de Gennes completed his PhD in 1957 (age 25) and was working as a research engineer at the French Atomic Energy Commission (CEA Saclay). His Nobel-winning work on liquid crystals and polymers began in 1968 (age 36). His PhD on neutron scattering, while competent, was not a seminal publication.
early_history_summary: Born in 1932 in Paris, de Gennes spent much of his childhood in the Alps due to health problems, receiving much of his basic education at home. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure (1951-1955), then worked as a research engineer at CEA Saclay (1955-1959), completing his PhD in 1957 on neutron scattering by critical-point fluctuations in ferromagnets. He did a postdoc at Berkeley with Charles Kittel in 1959 before serving in the French Navy.
family_context_summary: Parents met during WWI; father was a doctor who died in 1941. Mother raised him with strict principles. Childhood marked by health problems and wartime family separation. No evidence of significant financial privilege.
evidence_summary: De Gennes attended the elite ENS and completed a PhD by 25, but his Nobel-winning contributions to soft matter physics came after 1968 when he switched to liquid crystals. His early work on neutron scattering at CEA Saclay was not seminal. The PhD alone does not constitute a material milestone per the rubric.

name: Amancio Ortega
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Ortega worked as a shop hand and tailor from age 14 but did not found his first company, Confecciones Goa, until 1963 (age 27). His first Zara store opened in 1975 (age 39).
early_history_summary: Born in 1936 in Busdongo de Arbas, León, Spain, Ortega was the son of a railway worker. The family struggled financially, and Ortega left school at age 14 to work as a shop hand at a local shirtmaker called Gala in A Coruña, learning to make clothes by hand. He gathered experience with various retailers through the 1950s and early 1960s before founding his first manufacturing company in 1963.
family_context_summary: Son of a railway worker; family struggled financially, with Ortega recalling the shame of his mother being denied credit at a grocery store. Poverty was a motivating factor but not a platform of advantage.
evidence_summary: Ortega started working in garment shops at 14 and accumulated practical retail and manufacturing experience, but his first company (Confecciones Goa) was founded in 1963 at age 27, just past the age-26 cutoff. His Zara empire came even later in 1975. While he had significant domain exposure by 26, he had not yet achieved a material commercial milestone.

name: Arthur B. McDonald
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; McDonald earned a BSc (1964, age 21) and MSc (1965, age 22) from Dalhousie, and a PhD from Caltech in 1969 (age 26). His PhD alone does not constitute a material milestone, and his Nobel-winning neutrino oscillation work at SNO came in the 2000s.
early_history_summary: Born in 1943 in Sydney, Nova Scotia, Canada, McDonald was the son of an army officer. He entered Dalhousie University at 17 to study science, discovering a talent for physics. He earned a BSc in 1964 and MSc in 1965, with his master's work on positron lifetimes in metals producing a notably cited paper. He then pursued a PhD at Caltech under Charles Barnes, completing it in 1969, followed by a research position at Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories.
family_context_summary: Son of an army officer who participated in the liberation of the Netherlands and later served as a city councillor. Middle-class background with no noted financial privilege or disadvantage.
evidence_summary: McDonald followed a standard academic path through Dalhousie and Caltech, completing his PhD at 26. While his master's thesis paper on positron lifetimes became highly cited, it was not a seminal or field-defining publication. His Nobel Prize came from SNO experiments in the 2000s, decades after age 26.

name: Michel Mayor
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Mayor earned a master's in physics in 1966 (age 24) and a certificate in astronomy in 1968 (age 26). His PhD was awarded in 1971 (age 29) and his Nobel-winning exoplanet discovery (51 Pegasi b) came in 1995 (age 53).
early_history_summary: Born in 1942 in Lausanne, Switzerland, Mayor was inspired by an exceptional science teacher in secondary school. He studied physics and mathematics at the University of Lausanne, earning a master's in theoretical physics in 1966, then shifted to astrophysics at the University of Geneva, obtaining a certificate in astronomy in 1968 and a PhD in 1971 on stellar kinematics in the solar vicinity.
family_context_summary: Father was a police commissioner. Middle-class professional family background in Switzerland. No evidence of significant financial privilege or disadvantage.
evidence_summary: Mayor's path was a conventional academic trajectory through Lausanne and Geneva, with a PhD at 29. His Nobel-winning discovery of 51 Pegasi b came in 1995 at age 53. By age 26 he held only a master's degree and an astronomy certificate, with no seminal publications or notable discoveries.

name: Robert Coleman Richardson
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Richardson earned a BS (1958, age 21) and MS (1960, age 23) from Virginia Tech, and was a PhD student at Duke University by age 26. His PhD was awarded in 1966 (age 29) and his Nobel-winning discovery of superfluidity in helium-3 came in 1972 (age 35).
early_history_summary: Born in 1937 in Washington, D.C., Richardson grew up in Arlington, Virginia, and attended Virginia Polytechnic Institute (Virginia Tech), earning BS and MS degrees in physics. He served six months in the Army before enrolling in the PhD program at Duke University in low-temperature physics under Horst Meyer, working on NMR studies of solid helium-3. His PhD was completed in 1966, after which he joined David Lee's lab at Cornell.
family_context_summary: Father was a telephone company lineman who left college during the Great Depression due to family expenses. Working-class background with no evidence of financial privilege.
evidence_summary: Richardson followed a standard academic path through Virginia Tech and Duke, with his PhD completed at 29. His Nobel-winning discovery of superfluid helium-3 came in 1972 at age 35, nearly a decade past the age-26 threshold. By 26 he was a graduate student with no notable publications or discoveries.

name: Ada Yonath
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Yonath completed a BSc (1962, age 23) and MSc (1964, age 25) at Hebrew University, and was a PhD student at the Weizmann Institute by age 26. Her PhD was awarded in 1968 (age 29) and her Nobel-winning ribosome structure work began in the late 1970s.
early_history_summary: Born in 1939 in Jerusalem to a poor family, Yonath's father died when she was 11, forcing her to work cleaning and tutoring to support the family. Despite poverty, she attended prestigious schools and served in the Medical Corps before studying chemistry, biochemistry, and biophysics at Hebrew University (BSc 1962, MSc 1964). She began her PhD at the Weizmann Institute in 1964, working on collagen structure by X-ray crystallography.
family_context_summary: Born to poor Jewish parents in Jerusalem; family shared a cramped apartment with other families. Father died when she was 11, and she worked to support the family. Despite poverty, parents prioritized education and sent her to prestigious schools.
evidence_summary: Yonath overcame childhood poverty and the loss of her father to pursue chemistry at Hebrew University and crystallography at the Weizmann Institute. Her PhD was completed in 1968 at age 29, and her pioneering ribosome crystallography work began in the late 1970s. By age 26 she was a PhD student with no seminal publications or notable discoveries.

name: M. Stanley Whittingham
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Whittingham completed his BA and DPhil at Oxford by 1967 (age 26). His PhD alone does not constitute a material milestone. His seminal work on intercalation electrodes and lithium batteries at Exxon came in the 1970s, and his Young Author Award from the Electrochemical Society was in 1971 (age 30).
early_history_summary: Born in 1941 in Nottingham, England, Whittingham was the son of a civil engineer father and a chemist mother. He attended Stamford School and entered New College, Oxford in 1960 to study chemistry. His undergraduate research on tungsten oxide bronzes, supported by the US Air Force, resulted in his first publication in the Transactions of the Faraday Society. He completed his DPhil at Oxford in 1967 on solid-state chemistry, then took a postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford in 1968.
family_context_summary: Father was a civil engineer (first in his family to attend college) and mother was a chemist before marriage. Professional middle-class family with some domain proximity to science.
evidence_summary: Whittingham completed his DPhil at Oxford by 1967 (age 26) and had published a paper during his undergraduate years, but neither constituted a seminal publication or significant discovery. His Nobel-winning work on lithium-ion battery intercalation chemistry was conducted at Exxon in the 1970s, well beyond age 26. His first major recognition (Young Author Award) came in 1971 at age 30.
